titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

titolo: CVE-2026-100229: A flaw was found in GStreamer's H.266 codec parser library (libgstcodecparsers). An out-of-bounds wr...
descrizione: A flaw was found in GStreamer's H.266 codec parser library (libgstcodecparsers). An out-of-bounds write vulnerability exists in the DCI parsing function, where a reserved field value is incorrectly accepted, causing the parser to write beyond the bounds of an internal structure. An attacker could exploit this by providing a specially crafted H.266 bitstream to a third-party application that uses this library API, potentially causing a crash or memory corruption. No standard GStreamer pipeline element currently invokes the affected code path.

The zone file must be fed to NSD directly, (but it could come, for example, from an operator controlled provisioning system).

CVE-2026-103904: The public consent endpoint of JTL-Shop accepts arbitrary
consent names from unauthenticated visitor...
descrizione:
The public consent endpoint of JTL-Shop accepts arbitrary
consent names from unauthenticated visitors without validating
them against the configured consent items. These names are stored in the consent
statistics and rendered without output encoding in the administration
backend. An unauthenticated remote attacker can thereby inject script code that
is executed in the browser session of an administrator viewing the consent
statistics page, allowing actions to be performed with the administrator's
privileges.

titolo:
CVE-2026-103905: The authentication middleware of the JTL-Shop
administration backend processes the plugin safe mode ...
descrizione:
The authentication middleware of the JTL-Shop
administration backend processes the plugin safe mode toggle on the admin
logout route before checking whether the requesting user is
authenticated. An unauthenticated remote attacker can therefore switch the shop's
plugin safe mode on and off, which deactivates all installed plugins and their
functionality, such as payment and shipping integrations, resulting in a shop-wide
denial of service. The attack requires a single request and can be
automated against many installations.

titolo:
CVE-2026-104795: The insights-runtime-extractor runs as a privileged DaemonSet (`hostPID: true`)
that scans container...
descrizione:
The insights-runtime-extractor runs as a privileged DaemonSet (`hostPID: true`)
that scans container processes for runtime fingerprinting. When scanning a
container, the coordinator:

1. **fork()s** a child process
2. **setns()** into the target container's PID and mount namespaces
3. **fchdir()** back to an orphaned FD pointing at the extractor's own root
   filesystem (where `/crio.sock` is hostPath-mounted)
4. Calls **only `seteuid(target_uid)`** — changing the effective UID but leaving
   the **real UID and saved-set-UID at 0** and **retaining the permitted
   capability set**
5. The `check_no_privileged_perms()` guard inspects only the Effective capability
   set (so it passes), and is **skipped entirely when the target runs as uid 0**
6. The `VersionExecutable` fingerprint invokes `fpr_kind_executable` with
   `process.command_line[0]` — the target's argv[0], read from
   `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and **fully controlled by the workload**
7. `fpr_kind_executable` calls `exec.Command(executable, "--version").Output()`
   — executing the **workload's own binary** inside the workload's mount
   namespace while **ruid=0 in the host user namespace**

The executed process can call `setuid(0)` to restore full root with
`CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, and inherits the orphaned cwd which resolves into the extractor
container's filesystem containing the host CRI-O socket.

## Affected Code

### 1. Insufficient privilege drop (Rust — extractor coordinator)

**File:** `extractor/src/insights_runtime_extractor.rs`

```rust
// Lines 139-146 — seteuid-only drop, guard skipped for root containers
join_process_namespaces(process.pid)?;
change_dir(current_dir);
switch_user(*process.uid)?;
if *process.uid != 0 {
    perms::check_no_privileged_perms()
        .expect("Must not have privileged permissions to run fingerprints");
}
fingerprint::run_fingerprints(&config, out_dir, &process);
```

```rust
// Lines 182-185 — only effective UID changed; ruid/suid stay 0
fn switch_user(uid: u32) -> Result<(), ScannerError> {
    debug!("... Becoming user: {uid}");
    seteuid(uid.into()).map_err(|e| ScannerError::Errno(e))
}
```

### 2. Execution of untrusted binary (Go — fingerprint)

**File:** `fingerprints/pkg/utils/file.go`

```go
// Lines 75-80 — executes a path taken verbatim from workload's argv[0]
func GetExecutableVersionOutput(executable string) (string, error) {
    out, err := exec.Command(executable, "--version").Output()
    if err != nil {
        return "", err
    }
    return string(out), nil
}
```

### 3. Workload-controlled path forwarded (Rust — version_executable)

**File:** `version_executable.rs`

```rust
// Lines 29-34 — workload-controlled command_line[0] forwarded to fingerprint
return Some(vec![
    fpr_kind_executable,
    out_dir.to_string(),
    String::from(&process.command_line[0]),
    String::from(&version_executable.runtime_kind_name),
]);
```

## Attack Pattern

**Attacker:** Any tenant able to schedule a pod (unprivileged, any namespace)
**Victim:** The node running the insights-runtime-extractor DaemonSet
**Trigger:** Automatic — the DaemonSet scans all container processes on the node

**Attack sequence:**

1. Attacker creates a pod whose process name matches a configured
   versioned-executable pattern (`node`, `python`, `python3`, `MainThread`,
   or contains `java`)
2. The pod's main binary (at the path matching argv[0]) is a malicious
   executable that calls `setuid(0)` to restore root
3. When the insights operator triggers a scan, the DaemonSet forks, enters the
   attacker's mount namespace, and executes the attacker's binary with ruid=0
4. The attacker's code regains full root with `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` in the host user
   namespace
5. The inherited cwd contains the host CRI-O socket → full node compromise

titolo: CVE-2026-108072: Vulnerability due to incorrect permissions in TSplus Remote Access shared login scripts. The autosta...
descrizione: Vulnerability due to incorrect permissions in TSplus Remote Access shared login scripts. The autostart1.tscr files, located in the shared themes directory, allow users without sufficient privileges to write to them. A local attacker with a valid session on the terminal or remote desktop server could modify these files to execute arbitrary commands within another user’s security context when that user logs in using the same theme or operating mode. Depending on the affected user’s privileges, exploitation could allow lateral movement between users or privilege escalation.

The form's confirmation is delivered and its notification emails are sent even though no order exists at the payment provider and no payment is recorded.

titolo: GHSA-x32g-jvvm-4725: A2A Java SDK: Push notification credentials logged in cleartext on protobuf parse failure
descrizione:
### *Impact.** Push notification bearer tokens and authentication credentials submitted by clients are written to server log files in cleartext. Any operator, log aggregation system, or attacker with log access can read these secrets and use them to authenticate to the client's push notification endpoints, potentially sending forged task status updates.

**Where.** `transport/rest/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/transport/rest/handler/RestHandler.java:676` in `parseRequestBody`

**What.** The `parseRequestBody` method logs the entire JSON request body at `SEVERE` level when `JsonFormat.parser().merge()` throws `InvalidProtocolBufferException`. This method is called from `createTaskPushNotificationConfiguration` (line 377), where the body contains client-supplied push notification bearer tokens (field `token`) and authentication credentials (field `authentication.credentials`). These secrets are written to server log files in full.

**Exploit scenario.** A client creates a push notification configuration by POSTing to `/v1/tenants/{tenant}/tasks/{taskId}/pushNotificationConfigs` with a body containing `{"url": "https://client.example.com/webhook", "token": "secret-bearer-token", "authentication": {"scheme": "Bearer", "credentials": "oauth-access-token"}, "extraField": "value"}`. The extra field causes `JsonFormat.parser().merge()` to throw `InvalidProtocolBufferException`. The entire body including `secret-bearer-token` and `oauth-access-token` is logged at SEVERE level. An attacker with log access retrieves the cleartext credentials.

**Preconditions.**
- Attacker must have access to server log files (centralized logging, log aggregation, shared infrastructure, or insider access)
- Push notification capability must be enabled
- A request body must fail protobuf deserialization while being valid JSON (unknown fields with strict parsing, schema mismatches)

**Fix.** Do not log the raw request body. Log only a sanitized summary — body length and content type, not content. Replace the log call with something like: `log.log(Level.SEVERE, "Error parsing JSON request body (length={0})", body != null ? body.length() : 0)`.

**Verification.** 3/3 lens verifiers confirmed.

titolo: GHSA-4fpj-g9jf-9rgg: A2A Java SDK: Android synchronous POST forwards credentials across authorities after incomplete redirect fix
descrizione:
The GHSA-9rhm fix added this safe setting in
AndroidA2AHttpClient.createConnection():

    connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(false);

The synchronous POST builder later overwrites it:

    private boolean followRedirects = true;

    public A2AHttpResponse post() throws IOException {
        HttpURLConnection connection = createConnection("POST", false);
        connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(followRedirects);
        // ...
    }

The second assignment wins. JSONRPCTransport and RestTransport both
add interceptor-produced headers and call synchronous post() without
setting followRedirects(false).

On Android's repackaged OkHttp implementation, a cross-authority
redirect strips Authorization but retains nonstandard request headers.
AuthInterceptor permits four nonstandard authentication header names:

    X-API-Key
    API-Key
    X-Auth-Token
    X-Authentication

I confirmed that the exact v1.3.1.Final Maven artifact forwards
complete synthetic values under all four names to a second loopback
authority. I also reproduced the supported AuthInterceptor to Android
POST path. Explicitly calling followRedirects(false) returns the
original 302 and produces no request to the collector.

All test traffic stayed on two ephemeral 127.0.0.1 listeners. All
credentials were synthetic FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-* values.

Reproduction

I have attached AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest.java. Copy it to:

    extras/http-client-android/src/test/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/http/android/

Run:

    mvn -pl extras/http-client-android -am \
      -Dtest=AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest \
      -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false test

On unpatched current main, the default test fails with:

    Android synchronous POST must retain the documented no-redirect default
    expected: <302> but was: <200>

The explicit followRedirects(true) control still passes.

The separate exact-artifact fixture passed three consecutive runs. Its
relevant output was:

    default status=200 x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-DIRECT
authorization=null method=GET
    control-followRedirects-false status=302 collectorHits=0
    interceptor-chain status=200
x-api-key=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-INTERCEPTOR collectorHits=1
    header-matrix name=X-API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-API-Key
    header-matrix name=API-Key forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-API-Key
    header-matrix name=X-Auth-Token forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Auth-Token
    header-matrix name=X-Authentication
forwarded=FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-X-Authentication

Impact and limitations

The demonstrated impact is disclosure of a complete API key or
authentication token to a different authority. I am not claiming
subsequent use of the credential, integrity impact, availability
impact, code execution, or host compromise.

A fully malicious origin already receives the credential on the first
request. The additional boundary matters most when redirect or
front-door behavior is compromised separately from the component that
handles request credentials, or when different parts of the origin
operate in different trust domains.

The 7.5 score applies to an autonomous client where no human action is
needed after the remote endpoint returns the redirect. If the Android
workflow requires a person to select or invoke the remote agent, UI:R
gives a 6.5 score. I have kept both vectors because that deployment
detail affects severity but not the underlying behavior. These are
suggested scores, consistent with the policy's statement that actual
CVSS depends on the specific deployment context. The same policy
labels the parent credential-redirect property as moderate.

Scope and prior art

This path appears to fall directly under the project's current security model:

1. extras/http-client-android and the client transports are listed as in scope.
2. Remote AgentCard and response data are treated as attacker-relevant inputs.
3. A malicious or compromised remote agent is part of the client-side
adversary model.
4. Section 8 says automatic redirects are disabled in all JDK, Vert.x,
and Android implementations to prevent credential leakage.
5. Section 13 defines a violation of a Section 8 property through the
covered input and adversary as VALID.
6. Section 13a lists missed call sites and under-strength mitigations
as new findings after an incomplete fix.
7. Section 14 records the original issue as fixed by disabling
redirects across all HTTP client implementations. The Android
synchronous path directly contradicts that recorded repair state.

This report does not claim that an AgentCard SecurityScheme
declaration enforces authentication. The application has already
configured the credential, and the shipped AuthInterceptor places it
in an allowed header. The failure is the Android client's default
redirect behavior after that point. It does not depend on a custom
SPI, an insecure configuration flag, a test-only component,
server-side authentication, or any of the recurring non-findings
listed in Section 11a.

GHSA-9rhm is the direct parent finding. Its fix commit says redirects
were disabled across all clients, but the Android POST-level override
remains in 1.3.0.Final, 1.3.1.Final, and current main. I searched the
public issues and pull requests on September 5 and found PR #1097, but
no report covering this surviving synchronous Android path. The other
three published advisories address server authorization defaults,
push-notification SSRF, and credential logging. They do not cover this
Android client path.

Suggested fix

The smallest compatible change is:

    - private boolean followRedirects = true;
    + private boolean followRedirects = false;

This keeps followRedirects(true) available as an explicit opt-in. The
attached regression passes three out of three times after the change.
The Android module and its reactor dependencies pass 455 tests with no
failures. The full repository test run passes 2,914 tests with no
failures or errors. It reports 127 skips when using the project's
documented -DskipDockerTests=true option inside the isolated build
container.

Triage and incomplete-fix rules:
https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/SECURITY.md#L547-L573

Android documentation:
https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/docs/content/dev/security.md#L60-L74

Safe connection setting and later POST override:

https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-java/blob/30e31086e24bea096b5f662088661269c9119100/client/transport/spi/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/transport/spi/interceptors/auth/AuthInterceptor.java#L33-L46

titolo: GHSA-q78c-5jjq-57g8: A2A Java SDK has Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in push-notification delivery
descrizione:
---

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Affected package:** `org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common` (push-notification delivery)
- **Affected versions:** `<= 1.2.0.Final` (and `1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT` on `main` prior to the fix)
- **Patched version:** _(the release that carries the fix)_
- **CWE:** CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery)
- **Severity:** High
- **CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:L/A:N` (5.8, Moderate)

---

## Summary

An **unauthenticated** attacker can coerce the a2a-java server into issuing HTTP requests to
arbitrary internal and cloud-metadata endpoints from the server's own network position — a
Server-Side Request Forgery reachable in the default deployment with no credentials, no user
interaction, and a single request. The behaviour is the shipped default, not a misconfiguration.

## Details

`BasePushNotificationSender` (in `server-common`) POSTs task data to the URL stored on a task's
`TaskPushNotificationConfig` with no validation of the destination: no block on loopback, RFC1918,
link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, including the `169.254.169.254` metadata address), unique-local,
unspecified, or multicast ranges; no scheme restriction; and no bound on redirects.
`InMemoryPushNotificationConfigStore.setInfo` stores the URL verbatim and
`onCreateTaskPushNotificationConfig` does not check it either.

Both shipped HTTP clients follow redirects (`JdkA2AHttpClient` → `followRedirects(NORMAL)`,
`VertxA2AHttpClient` → `setFollowRedirects(true)`), so a creation-time URL allowlist is bypassable:
an attacker webhook answers `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/...` and the client follows it. A
hostname check is likewise defeated by DNS rebinding. A correct guard must validate the *resolved*
IP of every hop at connection time, not the URL string.

## Exploitation

Demonstrated end-to-end against a running server (default wiring, unauthenticated caller):

- **Arbitrary internal reachability.** The attacker picks the destination and the server issues
  the request from inside the trust boundary. Delivery to loopback and to a real RFC1918 LAN
  address was exercised at runtime; because the code applies no destination filtering of any kind,
  the same path reaches link-local / metadata (`169.254.169.254`) and other internal ranges
  wherever network routing permits.
- **Allowlist + method bypass via redirect.** A `302` from the attacker's webhook reaches
  destinations a creation-time allowlist would block, and a `302` on a `POST` is followed as a
  `GET` — so GET-only endpoints such as the IMDS credentials path are reachable even though the
  sender only issues `POST`s. This is why a URL allowlist is not a sufficient fix; the guard must
  validate the resolved IP of every redirect hop.
- **Data push into internal services.** On direct (non-redirected) delivery, each request carries
  the task payload in the body, so internal services that ingest POST data receive
  attacker-influenced content (basis for `I:L`). On a redirected request the body is dropped in the
  POST→GET conversion, so the body-push and the redirect-reach are separate capabilities, not
  simultaneous on one request.

The sender discards the fetched response and exposes no caller-visible difference between a
successful and a failed delivery (both paths return without surfacing status or body), so the base
case reads back nothing — confidentiality is scored `C:N`. Read-back is limited, reach is not: the
attacker still drives fully controlled requests to metadata and internal services and writes data
into them.

## PoC

Against a running server with push notifications enabled (JSON-RPC transport), using only the real
production classes wired the default way:

1. Start a local listener standing in for an internal target (no real metadata service is touched).
2. Send one `SendMessage` that starts a long-running task, with the push config inlined and its
   `url` set to `http://<internal-target>/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. Use
   `returnImmediately: true`, header `A2A-Version: 1.0`, and role `ROLE_USER`. The URL is stored
   verbatim. (Equivalent via `CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig` on an existing task.)
3. As the task emits state/artifact updates, the sender POSTs each one to the stored URL, from the
   server's own network position:

   ```
   POST /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ HTTP/1.1
   Host: 169.254.169.254
   Content-Type: application/json

   {"artifactUpdate":{"taskId":"...","artifact":{"parts":[{"text":"Progress update 1/20"}]}, ...}}
   ```

One `SendMessage` produced multiple server-side POSTs to the attacker-chosen internal path.
Verified on `main` (commit `72d220c`, JDK 21) and unchanged on `1.2.0.Final`.

## Remediation

Validate the *resolved* IP of the target and of every redirect hop before connecting: reject
loopback / RFC1918 / link-local / metadata / unique-local / unspecified / multicast; restrict the
scheme to `http`/`https`; cap redirects; and resolve-and-pin to defeat DNS rebinding. Enable by
default, with a documented opt-out for deployments that intentionally target internal webhooks. The
Go A2A SDK ships a dial-time resolved-IP guard of this shape by default.

**Workaround:** until a fixed release, block the host's outbound egress to the metadata endpoint
and internal ranges at the network layer.

## References

- CWE-918: Server-Side Request Forgery: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/918.html

titolo: GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w: A2A Java SDK has a fail-open default task authorization
descrizione:
Draft text for GHSA-qw47-mcm5-934w. The body below drops into the GitHub advisory description
field; the metadata block maps to the form fields. Set the patched version at release; publish
when the fix ships._

---

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Affected package:** `org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common` (task store / authorization)
- **Affected versions:** `<= 1.2.0.Final` (and `1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT` on `main` prior to the fix)
- **Patched version:** _(the release that carries the fix, e.g. 1.2.1.Final)_
- **CWE:** CWE-1188 (Insecure Default Initialization), CWE-862 (Missing Authorization)
- **Severity:** High
- **CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` (7.5, High)

---

## Details

The default task store performs no authorization on task reads. `InMemoryTaskStore`'s no-arg
constructor sets `authorizationProvider = null`, and `InMemoryTaskStore.get(String taskId)` is a
bare map lookup with no authorization check regardless of provider:

```java
public InMemoryTaskStore() {
    this.authorizationProvider = null;   // default wiring
}

@Override
public @Nullable Task get(String taskId) {
    return tasks.get(taskId);            // no owner / caller check
}
```

Authorization is enforced only when the application both supplies a `TaskAuthorizationProvider`
*and* routes requests through `AuthorizationRequestHandlerDecorator` (via CDI), which checks
ownership before delegating. A server that uses the default store, or wires
`DefaultRequestHandler.builder().build()` manually, or integrates through a non-CDI stack (e.g.
Spring), never reaches that check. The safe posture is therefore opt-in and the shipped default is
the unsafe one. A caller can read a task created by another caller simply by knowing or guessing
its id.

## Summary

With the SDK's default configuration, task reads are not authorized: any caller can retrieve a
task (including its status, context, message history, and artifacts) created by another caller,
by supplying the task id.

## PoC

Using only the real production classes wired the default way (no mocks):

1. Construct the default store: `InMemoryTaskStore store = new InMemoryTaskStore();` (no-arg
   constructor, so no authorization provider).
2. As one caller, save a task: `store.save(victimTask, false);` with id `victim-task-42`.
3. As a second, unrelated caller with no auth context, read it back: `store.get("victim-task-42")`.

The second caller receives the first caller's task in full, with no authorization check:

```
unauthenticated get(victim-task-42) returned task owned by nobody-checked: victim-task-42 / ctx=victim-ctx
```

Verified on `main` (commit `72d220c`, JDK 21) and reproduces unchanged on `1.2.0.Final`.

## Impact

Task data crosses caller boundaries with no authorization. In any multi-caller deployment built on
the default wiring, one caller can enumerate and read another caller's tasks, including task status,
context id, the message history, and any artifacts the task carries, which for agent workloads is
frequently sensitive input and generated content. Because the insecure behaviour is the default
rather than a misconfiguration, it is easy to ship unintentionally, and in the default/reference
deployment the transport endpoints are served without authentication enforced, so the read is
reachable by an unauthenticated caller (`PR:N`). CVSS is scored against the default configuration
as shipped.

## Remediation

Fail closed by default: deny task reads when no authorization provider is configured, rather than
treating a missing provider as allow-all, and apply the authorization check in the store's `get`
path (not only in `list` and the CDI decorator) so it holds regardless of how the handler is
wired. If the current permissive default is retained for single-user/testing scenarios, emit a
prominent startup warning when the server comes up with no authorization provider so it cannot be
shipped by accident.

## Workarounds

Until a fixed release, configure a `TaskAuthorizationProvider` and ensure requests are routed
through the authorization decorator (CDI wiring), rather than relying on the default no-arg store
or a manually built handler.

## References

- CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1188.html
- CWE-862: Missing Authorization: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/862.html

titolo: GHSA-9rhm-2h4x-jwmx: A2A Java SDK send client credentials under server-controlled HTTP header name, enabling leakage via redirect
descrizione:
*Impact.** A malicious or compromised A2A agent can cause the client's API key credential to be forwarded to an arbitrary third-party server. The agent serves an AgentCard with an `APIKeySecurityScheme` specifying a custom header name, then responds with an HTTP redirect. The JDK HttpClient follows the redirect and forwards the custom header containing the credential, since only the standard `Authorization` header may be stripped on cross-origin redirects.

**Where.** `client/transport/spi/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/transport/spi/interceptors/auth/AuthInterceptor.java:69` in `intercept`

**What.** The `apiKeySecurityScheme.name()` field from the remote agent's AgentCard (untrusted, server-controlled data) is used directly as the HTTP header name when placing client credentials. Combined with `JdkA2AHttpClient`'s `followRedirects(NORMAL)` policy, credentials under custom header names survive cross-origin redirects (only `Authorization` is stripped on newer JDKs), allowing a malicious agent to leak client credentials to third-party servers. Additionally, `AuthInterceptor` does not check that `location==HEADER` before placing the credential as a header.

**Exploit scenario.** Client configures an API key credential for agent's security scheme `myAuth`. The malicious agent returns an AgentCard where `securitySchemes` includes `myAuth` as `APIKeySecurityScheme` with `name='X-Leaked-Cred'` and `location=HEADER`. `AuthInterceptor` places the credential in the `X-Leaked-Cred` header. The agent responds with HTTP 302 redirect to `https://evil.com/collect`. `JdkA2AHttpClient` follows the redirect, forwarding all custom headers including `X-Leaked-Cred` to `evil.com`. The attacker captures the client's credential.

**Preconditions.**
- Client application has configured API key credentials via `CredentialService` for the agent's security scheme
- The agent is malicious or compromised (controls its own AgentCard response)
- The default `JdkA2AHttpClient` is used (with `followRedirects=NORMAL`)
- The JDK version does not strip custom headers on cross-origin redirects (all current versions)

**Fix.** Validate the `APIKeySecurityScheme.name()` field against a whitelist of safe header names. Check that `apiKeySecurityScheme.location()` equals `Location.HEADER` before placing the credential as a header. Consider using `followRedirects(NEVER)` and implementing manual redirect handling that strips all authentication headers on cross-origin redirects.

**Verification.** 2/3 lens verifiers confirmed.

titolo: GHSA-58r4-6rv3-gfh8: Pillow: Out-of-bounds access in _imagingmorph on a zero-width image
descrizione:
### Summary
A PPM or PGM file can declare a width of 0, which Pillow accepts, producing an image of size `(0, N)`. Passing that image to `ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply()` makes the native morphology code index a row buffer at `outrow[width - 1]`, which is `outrow[-1]` when the width is 0. The process crashes.

### Details
The PPM parser reads width and height with no lower-bound check:

- `src/PIL/PpmImagePlugin.py:119`

The native `apply()` writes the row edges with no guard that the width is positive:

- `src/_imagingmorph.c:81` sets `outrow[0] = outrow[width - 1] = 0;`

`match()` and `get_on_pixels()` use the same edge-indexing pattern.

### PoC
```python
from PIL import Image, ImageMorph

# A width-0 image (also producible from a crafted PPM header). apply() indexes
# outrow[width - 1] == outrow[-1] in native code.
im = Image.new("L", (0, 5))
ImageMorph.MorphOp(op_name="dilation4").apply(im)
```

Run it:
```
$ python 03_poc.py
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96`.

Under AddressSanitizer:
```
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address (pc ... in apply)
    #0 apply   src/_imagingmorph.c:81
SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/_imagingmorph.c:81 in apply
```
With width 0 the `outrow[width - 1]` write lands on an unmapped page, so it surfaces as a SEGV pinned to the edge-write line rather than a redzone overflow.

### Impact
Out-of-bounds write in a C extension. Affects any application that runs a morphology operation on an image opened from untrusted input. Result is a crash and possible memory corruption.

titolo: GHSA-65qm-jvmh-6pqg: Pillow: GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS
descrizione:
``` ============================================================================ GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:293 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A GIF of about 60 bytes can make Pillow allocate gigabytes of memory. This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to `self._size` and only then calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()`. Nothing restores the old size when `DecompressionBombError` is raised, because `seek()` only rolls back on `EOFError`. After the caught error, `im.size` reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer `im.im` is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070. In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried `seek(1)` followed by `load()` then reaches `load_prepare()`, which calls `Image.core.fill()` with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. `Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...)` and `rotate(..., expand=True)` also allocate from the stale size. The default paths are unaffected: plain `Image.open()` plus `load()`, `ImageSequence.Iterator`, and `n_frames`/`is_animated`. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs the decompression-bomb check for the new size only *after* storing it on the object: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294 (GifImageFile._seek) x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) # state mutated Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) # ...then validated ``` `_decompression_bomb_check()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3586`) raises `DecompressionBombError` for anything above `2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178 956 970 px by default), but by then `self._size` already holds the rejected value and nothing restores it: `seek()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:166-179`) only rolls back on `EOFError`, and `_seek(0)` only ever grows `_size`. The object that the application still holds therefore reports `im.size == (40000, 40000)` while `im.im` is the 1×1 buffer of frame 0. Compare the two dispose-extent checks a few lines further down in the same function (`GifImagePlugin.py:383` and `:407`), which call `_decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size)` *before* the corresponding `Image.core.fill()`, and `TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321`), which checks `_tile_size` before allocating from it. With this 60-byte GIF (hex) ``` 47494638396101000100800000000000ffffff GIF89a, 1x1 screen, 2-entry global palette 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 frame 0: 1x1 @ (0,0), LZW data 2c00000000409c409c00 frame 1 descriptor: 40000x40000 @ (0,0) 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 another 1x1 frame 3b trailer ``` `Image.open()` succeeds (`im.size == (1, 1)`), `im.seek(1)` raises `DecompressionBombError: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels`, and afterwards `im.size == (40000, 40000)`, `im.im.size == (1, 1)`, `im.tell() == 0`. What happens next depends on what the application does with the object, but several ordinary operations take their dimensions from `im.size` rather than from the C buffer: - Retrying `im.seek(1)`. The failed `_seek` left `self.__offset == 0` and the file pointer just past the 9-byte descriptor, so the retry parses whatever follows — in the file above, a valid 1×1 frame — and succeeds. `im.load()` then runs `GifImageFile.load_prepare()`: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:452-456 elif self.mode in ("RGB", "RGBA"): self._prev_im = self.im if self._frame_palette: self.im = Image.core.fill("P", self.size, self._frame_transparency or 0) ``` which allocates and `memset`s a 40000×40000 "P" image (1.6 GB) to decode a 1×1 tile into, and `load_end()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:485-491`) fills a second one and converts it to RGB (another 1.6 GB + 6.4 GB). - `im.rotate(angle, expand=True)` for a non-multiple-of-90 angle, or the common flatten-onto-background idiom `Image.new("RGB", im.size, bg)`, allocate from `im.size` as well (measured on an object poisoned to 20000×20000: `rotate(45, expand=True)` completes and touches 776 MiB; `Image.new("RGB", im.size, "white")` touches 1.5 GiB). Operations that pass `im.size` as a box against the real buffer (`thumbnail`, `resize`, `save`) fail with `ValueError`/`SystemError` instead. The extent fields are 16-bit offset plus 16-bit size, so the stored size can be pushed to 131070×131070 (17.2 Gpx; 17 GB for mode "P", 69 GB for "RGB"/"RGBA" storage), 96× the error threshold. `n_frames` / `is_animated` are not affected: they call `_seek(frame, update_image=False)`, which skips the `_size` assignment (the file above reports `n_frames == 2`, `is_animated == True` and leaves `im.size` at 1×1). ## Impact A remote user who can upload a GIF to a service that (a) seeks animation frames and (b) catches the exception from `seek()` — a broad `except Exception` around a `while True: im.seek(im.tell()+1)` frame-collection loop, or an explicit `except DecompressionBombError: log and continue` — and then keeps using the same `Image` object, ends up driving allocations of 1.6 GB to tens of GB from a 60-byte file: `MemoryError` after the process has committed gigabytes, or an OOM kill of the worker when no address-space limit is set. The `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` guard fires, but does not actually keep the rejected dimensions out of the object it is guarding. The precondition is real application behaviour but not the default path: `Image.open(); im.load()` is unaffected, and `ImageSequence.Iterator` propagates the error out of the `for` statement (a `try` inside the loop body does not swallow it). Hence low severity. This is adjacent to the GIF extent bomb check added for CVE-2022-45198: the ordering was introduced with that check in `c9f1b35e9810` ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30), first released in Pillow 9.2.0. Before it, the same size growth happened with no check at all; the check introduced there is the one that runs too late. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script run against the installed Pillow. It needs about 1.7 GB of free RAM. 1. **`setup_env()`** caps the process address space at 3 GiB with `RLIMIT_AS`, so the oversized allocations end in `MemoryError` instead of the OOM killer. It then opens the 60-byte GIF shown above, built in memory by `bomb_gif()`. The GIF contains a 1×1 screen and a 1×1 frame 0, so `Image.open()` passes its own bomb check. Next comes a bare frame-1 image descriptor that declares 40000×40000 (1.6 Gpx, about 9× the error threshold). A real 1×1 frame follows it. 2. **`poc()`** calls `im.seek(1)` and catches `DecompressionBombError`, the way an application that skips bad frames would. 3. **First check: the state is inconsistent.** The script prints `im.size` next to the real pixel buffer `im.im.size`. If the rejected frame had left the object unchanged, both would be `(1, 1)`. On the affected code `im.size` is `(40000, 40000)`. 4. **Second check: memory use.** The script retries `im.seek(1)`, which now parses the trailing 1×1 frame, and calls `im.load()`. It prints the process's peak RSS before and after. `load_prepare()` sizes its `Image.core.fill()` from `im.size`, so loading a single pixel fills a 1.6 GB buffer before the 3 GiB cap stops the next allocation. Expected output on the affected tree: ``` open(): 60-byte GIF, size=(1, 1) seek(1) raised as intended: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels, could be decompression bomb DOS attack. after the caught error: im.size=(40000, 40000), pixel buffer im.im.size=(1, 1) seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap; peak RSS 18 MiB -> 1700 MiB BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only if both checks hold: the over-limit size stayed on the object after the exception, and peak RSS grew by more than 1000 MiB while loading a 1×1 frame. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, it prints `im.size=(1, 1)`, peak RSS stays at about 23 MiB, and the last line is `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch validates before mutating in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`): the enlarged extent is computed into a local, passed to `_decompression_bomb_check()`, and only then assigned to `self._size`, matching the order of the two `dispose_size` checks further down the same function. A rejected frame therefore leaves the object in its pre-seek state; valid files behave as before, and the exception is still raised at the same point: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py @@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile): x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: - self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) + size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) + Image._decompression_bomb_check(size) + self._size = size frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1 flags = s[8] ``` `n_frames` / `is_animated` go through `update_image=False` and are unaffected. The patch also extends `test_exception_gif_extents` in `Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py` to assert that `im.size` is unchanged after the `DecompressionBombError`. It does not change `seek()` itself; optionally, `seek()` could also treat `DecompressionBombError` like `EOFError` and re-seek to `last_frame`, so that a retried `seek()` does not resume parsing from the middle of the rejected frame. ## The patch GIF: run the decompression bomb check on an enlarging frame's extent before storing it in self._size Applies to `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py index 98d833736..83cc785fc 100644 --- a/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py +++ b/Tests/test_decompression_bomb.py @@ -63,6 +63,9 @@ class TestDecompressionBomb: with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): im.seek(1) + # The rejected frame should not have changed the image size + assert im.size == (100, 100) + def test_exception_gif_zero_width(self, monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: # Set limit to trigger exception on the test file monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", 4 * 64 * 128) diff --git a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py index 11fb180fc..f9bda06c2 100644 --- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py @@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile): x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: - self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) + size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) + Image._decompression_bomb_check(size) + self._size = size frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1 flags = s[8] ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,474 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # GifImageFile._seek() stores a frame's enlarged size in self._size and only # *then* runs the decompression-bomb check. The check raises, but the object # keeps the rejected 40000x40000 size over its real 1x1 pixel buffer, and the # next load() allocates from that size: 1.6+ GB for a 60-byte GIF. import io import resource import struct from PIL import Image BOMB = 40000 # 40000x40000 = 1.6 Gpx, ~9x the DecompressionBombError threshold LIMIT = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS def frame_1x1(): # image descriptor at (0,0) 1x1, then a 1-pixel LZW stream return b"," + struct.pack(" LIMIT and im.im.size == (1, 1) # Effect: retrying the seek lands on the real 1x1 frame, but load() sizes its # buffers from the poisoned im.size. before = peak_rss_mib() im.seek(1) try: im.load() outcome = "completed" except MemoryError: outcome = "MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap" after = peak_rss_mib() print(f"seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: {outcome}; peak RSS {before} MiB -> {after} MiB") ballooned = after - before > 1000 print("BUG" if poisoned and ballooned else "OK") ```

titolo: GHSA-vx6w-vv9f-6gvg: Pillow: EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit
descrizione:
``` ============================================================================ EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit Location: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:92 in Ghostscript() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application opens an untrusted Encapsulated PostScript file and asks Pillow to render it at a larger scale, Pillow has Ghostscript produce an image several times bigger than Pillow's configured size limit allows. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file. The cause is in `Ghostscript()` in `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's `scale` (lines 93-94) and passes the product to `gs` as the `-g` output geometry. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption. The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons: * The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file. * With the default warning filter, `Image.open()` already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at `scale=1`. * Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since `gs` runs with no timeout. This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF `load(dpi)` gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing `Image.open()` and reaching `gs` with `-g18000x18000`. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included. ## Details `EpsImageFile.load(scale=N)` (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders `width*N × height*N` pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one `Image.open()` ran on the *unscaled*, file-declared `width × height`. The scaled product is never passed to `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` before `gs` is started. This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (89,478,485), so `Image.open()` accepts it without even a warning: ``` %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments 0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke showpage ``` `im.load(scale=2)` on it then executes ``` gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage ``` i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), whose `pnmraw` output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by `Image.open()` with `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is ever run; via `scale=2` the same raster is rendered first and the `DecompressionBombError` only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. (Between 1× and 2× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, `Image.open()` only emits `DecompressionBombWarning`, so with the default warning filter an EPS declaring e.g. 13377×13377 is already rendered at `scale=1` — a 537 MB PNM. Against that baseline, `scale=2` is 4× an already-permitted render.) The arithmetic is in `Ghostscript()`: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:91-97 # Hack to support hi-res rendering scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:139-142 command = [ gs_binary, "-q", # quiet mode f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}", # set output geometry (pixels) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:165-168 subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo) with Image.open(outfile) as out_im: out_im.load() return out_im.im.copy() ``` and its caller does nothing between taking `scale` from the application and invoking it: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:411-417 def load(self, scale: int = 1, transparency: bool = False) -> …: # Load EPS via Ghostscript if self.tile: assert self.fp is not None self.im = Ghostscript(self.tile, self.size, self.fp, scale, transparency) ``` `size` here is `self._size`, computed in `_open()` from the file's `%%BoundingBox` (or `%ImageData`) and checked once by `Image.open()` at `src/PIL/Image.py:3700`. For the benign path (`scale=1`) that check covers exactly what Ghostscript is asked to render. For `scale=N` the rendered pixel count is N² times what was checked, so a file can sit just under the limit at open time and have Ghostscript render 4× (scale 2), 9× (scale 3), 16× (scale 4) the configured budget. The first point at which Pillow looks at the real size again is `Image.open(outfile)` at line 166 — after `subprocess.check_call` has returned, i.e. after Ghostscript has spent the CPU and written `width*height*3` bytes to `tempfile.mkstemp()`'s directory. `WmfStubImageFile.load(dpi)` has the same shape (file-derived extent × caller-supplied factor → new raster) and, since af70b075a, calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)` on the recomputed size before rendering (`src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:127-131`). The EPS path lacks the equivalent line. The gap dates from ce2955ec7128 ("Throw an exception when an opened image is larger than an arbitrary limit", 2014-05-14, first released in 2.5.0), which added the check to `Image.open()` without covering the `scale` path. ## Impact Affected are applications that open untrusted EPS/PS with Ghostscript installed and call `load(scale=N)` with a fixed N > 1, as the handbook suggests for non-blurry output. Handing untrusted EPS to Ghostscript at all already lets the same attacker tie up a worker with an equally tiny file (e.g. a PostScript `{} loop`; Pillow runs `gs` with no timeout), so this bug adds a constant factor rather than a new denial-of-service capability. Within that setting, a ~110-byte upload makes each request run Ghostscript over N² × `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` pixels (N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` if the application does not turn `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error) and write a `W·H·3`-byte PNM into the temp directory — 972 MB for the example above at scale 2, 2.2 GB at scale 3, 8.6 GB for a 178-Mpixel declaration at scale 4 — before any limit is applied. The operator's `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` setting is exceeded by a factor of N²; N is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file, so the work stays bounded at N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because `Image.open(outfile)` re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption. This is a sibling of the WMF `load(dpi)` issue fixed in af70b075a ("Add decompression bomb check when loading at a different DPI"); the EPS `scale` path was not covered by that change. Unlike the WMF case, where the file-controlled `_inch` makes the ratio unbounded, the EPS multiplier is fixed by the application. ## Reproducing Run `repro` against the installed Pillow. Ghostscript does not need to be installed: the script sets `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs"` so that `has_ghostscript()` skips its `gs --version` probe, and replaces `subprocess.check_call` with a function that records the command line Pillow builds and then raises `OSError`, so nothing is actually rendered. It writes a 76-byte EPS declaring `%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000` (the example above without the drawing line; 81 Mpixel, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` of 89,478,485) and turns `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error, so any bomb check — warning or hard error — counts. It then calls `Image.open()` and `im.load(scale=2)`. `Image.open()` accepts the file and `load(scale=2)` reaches the intercepted Ghostscript call with `-g18000x18000` (324,000,000 pixels, 3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, a 972 MB `pnmraw` output with real Ghostscript). The script prints the geometry it captured. It prints `BUG` when Ghostscript was invoked with a `-g` geometry above `2*MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178,956,970) and no decompression-bomb check fired before that call; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, `load(scale=2)` raises `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is called and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch checks the scaled size in `Ghostscript()` right after the scaled `width`/`height` are computed (`src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:93-94`) and before the `gs` command is built, mirroring `WmfStubImageFile.load`: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` `load(scale=N)` now raises `DecompressionBombError` / emits `DecompressionBombWarning` under the same `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` thresholds `Image.open()` applies, before Ghostscript runs instead of after. Placing the check in `Ghostscript()` rather than in `EpsImageFile.load()` is the single point where the rendered extent is decided, so it also covers direct callers of the module-level function. With the patch applied to a clean checkout the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_file_eps.py` passes. One cosmetic side effect: at `scale=1` the check re-emits the `DecompressionBombWarning` that `Image.open()` already issued for sizes between 1× and 2× the limit; guarding the call with `if scale > 1:` would avoid the duplicate. The patch also adds `test_load_scale_decompression_bomb` to `Tests/test_file_eps.py`, in the style of the WMF test: it sets `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` to `im.width * im.height` and expects `im.load(scale=2)` to raise `DecompressionBombError`. Like the rest of that file it is skipped without Ghostscript, because `has_ghostscript()` is consulted at the top of `Ghostscript()`; moving the check above that call would let the test run without it. ## The patch Add decompression bomb check on the scaled size in EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() before Ghostscript is invoked Applies to `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_eps.py b/Tests/test_file_eps.py index 70eced62a..de331d97f 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_eps.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_eps.py @@ -98,6 +98,14 @@ def test_sanity(filename: str, size: tuple[int, int], scale: int) -> None: assert image.format == "EPS" +@pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") +def test_load_scale_decompression_bomb(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: + with Image.open(FILE1) as im: + monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", im.width * im.height) + with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): + im.load(scale=2) + + @pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") def test_load() -> None: with Image.open(FILE1) as im: diff --git a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py index 5eaefe339..ccc6f1d85 100644 --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,845 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript(): load(scale=N) hands gs a -g geometry of # (W*N)x(H*N) with no _decompression_bomb_check on the scaled size; only the # unscaled WxH was checked by Image.open(). gs is not installed here, so we # set gs_binary and intercept subprocess.check_call to read the argv Pillow builds. import os, subprocess, tempfile, warnings from PIL import Image, EpsImagePlugin EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs" # skip the `gs --version` probe path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.eps") with open(path, "w") as f: # 9000x9000 = 81 Mpx < MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89.5 Mpx) f.write("%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0\n%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000\n%%EndComments\nshowpage\n") calls = [] def fake_check_call(cmd, **kw): calls.append(cmd) raise OSError("gs intercepted") # stop here; we only need the argv subprocess.check_call = fake_check_call hard = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS bomb_before_gs = False with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("error", Image.DecompressionBombWarning) try: with Image.open(path) as im: print("Image.open accepted", os.path.getsize(path), "byte EPS, size", im.size) im.load(scale=2) except (Image.DecompressionBombError, Image.DecompressionBombWarning) as e: bomb_before_gs = not calls print("bomb check fired", "before" if bomb_before_gs else "after", "gs:", e) except OSError as e: print("load() reached gs:", e) over = False for c in calls: g = next(a for a in c if a.startswith("-g"))[2:] w, h = map(int, g.split("x")) over |= w * h > hard print(f"gs argv geometry -g{g} = {w*h} px ({w*h/Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS:.1f}x MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, " f"hard limit {hard}); pnmraw output would be {w*h*3} bytes") print("BUG" if calls and over and not bomb_before_gs else "OK") ```
